university: University of North Carolina at Charlotte

documents.title: Suggested Syllabus Policies & Notices
tiers: Option 1: AI permitted in all assignments with disclosure
Option 2: AI permitted only on designated assignments with disclosure
documents.summary: A university legal-affairs page of suggested syllabus notices. Its AI section offers two templates a faculty member can adopt (permit with attribution, or permit only as designated) and advises on AI detection tools and student consent.
documents.stance_why: The document does not choose a stance for the university; it offers two templates (permit all with attribution vs permit only on designated assignments) that 'may be used or adapted, depending on the level of generative AI use the faculty member wants to permit', so it delegates and lists the two as tiers.

units.why: The page says faculty 'should notify students how and when generative AI tools' may be used; a best-practice recommendation to instructors to communicate AI expectations, so P09 with actor instructor, course-start, should.
units.anchor: faculty members should notify students how and when generative AI tools
units.policy: Faculty should notify students how and when generative AI tools may be used in their assignments, exams, and other course work.

units.why: The two suggested policies are offered 'depending on the level of generative AI use the faculty member wants to permit', so the university sets no rule but gives a menu of levels; this is P05 (named options) while the choice rests with the instructor.
units.anchor: two suggested syllabus policies that may be used or adapted
units.policy: Two suggested syllabus policies, adaptable to the level of generative AI use the faculty member wants to permit, are offered.

units.why: Option 1 text: 'students are permitted to use generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools like Microsoft Copilot or Google Gemini'; default permission for all course work, so P02.
units.anchor: students are permitted to use generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools
units.policy: In this course, students are permitted to use generative AI tools like Microsoft Copilot or Google Gemini to support their work.

units.why: The template says students 'must disclose any AI-generated material they use and properly attribute it'; a disclosure and attribution duty, P24.
units.anchor: students must disclose any AI-generated material they use and properly attribute it
units.policy: Students must disclose any AI-generated material they use and properly attribute it, including in-text citations, quotations, and references.

units.why: The sentence makes students answerable for 'any errors or information that is misrepresented or inaccurate (i.e. hallucinations)'. It combines responsibility with the fallibility of AI; P31 is closest, and the accountability for errors is the fit note.
units.anchor: students are responsible for any errors or information that is misrepresented or inaccurate
units.policy: Students are responsible for any errors or inaccurate information (hallucinations) that generative AI tools produce when they submit work that includes AI-generated material.
units.fit_note: Stresses that students bear responsibility for AI errors in submitted work (accountability), not only that output may be wrong.

units.why: The template supplies an exact 'acknowledges the use of [generative AI tool Name]' statement naming the tool and how it was used; P25 (tool and manner details) fits better than generic P24.
units.anchor: acknowledges the use of [generative AI tool Name] in the preparation or completion
units.policy: Students include in their assignments a statement acknowledging the generative AI tool used and the way(s) it was used (for example brainstorming, grammatical correction, citation, which portion).
units.fit_note: Requires tool name and manner of use, not prompt or output.

units.why: The 'Important Note on Data Protection and Privacy' warns that 'there is no guarantee that the information you provide will remain confidential' and tells users to avoid sharing sensitive information; privacy, P50.
units.anchor: avoid sharing any sensitive or private information when using these tools
units.policy: Students should avoid sharing sensitive or private information (personally identifiable information, PHI, financial data, intellectual property, original research, legally protected data) with generative AI tools, because supplied data might be used for training and confidentiality is not guaranteed.

units.why: Option 2 limits AI to 'only for specific assignments, and only as designated by the instructor'; permission is per assignment, so the instructor sets the rule (P04). It is not P01 since AI is allowed where designated.
units.anchor: only for specific assignments, and only as designated by the instructor
units.policy: In this course, students are permitted to use generative AI tools only for specific assignments, and only as designated by the instructor.

units.why: Option 2 notes faculty 'should specifically indicate on each assignment whether generative AI is permitted, and the way in which it may be used'; an instruction to instructors to state expectations in assignment instructions, P09.
units.anchor: specifically indicate on each assignment whether generative AI is permitted
units.policy: Faculty members should specifically indicate on each assignment whether generative AI is permitted, and the way in which it may be used.

units.why: The phrase 'use of a generative AI tool that is not specifically authorized by the instructor may constitute a violation of the Code of Student Academic Integrity' classifies unauthorized AI use as misconduct, P36.
units.anchor: not specifically authorized by the instructor may constitute a violation of the
units.policy: Use of a generative AI tool that is not specifically authorized by the instructor may constitute a violation of the Code of Student Academic Integrity.

units.why: The generic template says listed tools 'are prohibited ... unless I explicitly permit such use'. It is about CourseHero and Chegg and points to the AI policies above; it is a default-prohibit-unless-permitted rule on unauthorized tools, but not about AI itself, so no AI type fits and I use UNCOVERED rather than P06.
units.anchor: are prohibited for completing course assignments, quizzes or examinations, or other academic exercises
units.policy: Listed materials, equipment, websites or tools are prohibited for completing course assignments, quizzes or examinations, or other academic exercises unless the instructor explicitly permits such use for legitimate pedagogical purposes.
units.uncovered_note: Template for prohibiting unauthorized third-party materials and websites (CourseHero, Chegg) unless the instructor permits them; not specifically about AI.

units.why: The detection section says tools like ZeroGPT are 'designated as DO NOT USE by OneIT' as they are error-prone and fail reliability standards; detectors are unreliable and should not be used, P39.
units.anchor: designated as DO NOT USE by OneIT
units.policy: Generative AI detection tools (such as ZeroGPT) are designated DO NOT USE by OneIT because no University enterprise tool is available or recommended.

units.why: The text says detection products 'are prone to error and do not meet reliability standards' and do not ensure privacy; this is the reasoning behind the ban and a statement of unreliability (P39); the privacy part is the fit note.
units.anchor: prone to error and do not meet reliability standards
units.policy: Both free and paid generative AI detection products are prone to error and do not meet reliability standards, and often do not sufficiently ensure the privacy of data input into them.
units.fit_note: Also says detection tools do not sufficiently protect the privacy of content entered into them.

units.why: 'such tools should not be relied on as presumptive of the use of generative AI' sets an evidence standard: detector output is not presumptive proof, which fits P69 (detector output not proof) better than P39 because it speaks to what counts as evidence.
units.anchor: should not be relied on as presumptive of the use of generative AI
units.policy: Generative AI detection tools should not be relied on as presumptive of the use of generative AI in completing an assignment.

units.why: Instructors who use a detector 'against University recommendations' must 'obtain a signed consent' to notify students and obtain FERPA consent and copyright permission; a consent condition on detection. No type is about student consent to detection tools, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: obtain a signed consent before submitting student work to a generative AI detection tool
units.policy: Before submitting student work to a generative AI detection tool, an instructor obtains a signed consent that notifies students of the tool and provides FERPA consent and copyright permission.
units.uncovered_note: Instructors must notify students and obtain signed FERPA and copyright consent before uploading their work to AI detection or plagiarism tools.

units.why: For students who refuse consent, the page advises not submitting their work to a detector and offering alternatives (reflection paper, draft bibliography, photocopied sources); nearest is P40 (process evidence), with the consent condition as fit note.
units.anchor: it is not advisable to submit their work to a plagiarism detection service
units.policy: If a student does not sign the consent form, it is not advisable to submit their work to a plagiarism or generative AI detection tool; instead the instructor offers alternatives such as a short reflection paper on research methodology, a draft bibliography, or photocopies of cited sources.
units.fit_note: Mainly says not to run the work through detectors without consent and gives process-evidence alternatives.

units.why: Suggested Option 1 syllabus text tells students all required work 'may be subject to submission' to a generative AI detection tool; a notice that detection is used, P40.
units.anchor: generative AI detection tool for detection of unauthorized use
units.policy: As a condition of taking the course, all required work may be submitted to SimCheck or another plagiarism service and/or a generative AI detection tool for detection of unauthorized use of generative AI, but not without the student's written consent.

units.why: Option 2 text applies detection only to work the instructor 'in good faith suspects' was created with unauthorized generative AI; a targeted use of detection tools, P40, with the suspicion threshold as fit note.
units.anchor: instructor in good faith suspects are in whole or in part created with
units.policy: Work that the instructor in good faith suspects was created in whole or in part with unauthorized use of a generative AI tool is subject to submission to a generative AI detection tool.
units.fit_note: Detection limited to work the instructor suspects in good faith.

units.why: 'Use of SimCheck ... is entirely in the discretion of the instructor' but needs advance syllabus notice and signed consent. This concerns plagiarism detection, not AI, and no type covers consent to plagiarism tools, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: entirely in the discretion of the instructor
units.policy: Use of SimCheck or another plagiarism detection service is entirely in the discretion of the instructor, but requires advance notice in the syllabus and a signed consent form from each student.
units.uncovered_note: Instructors who use SimCheck or other plagiarism detection must give advance syllabus notice and obtain signed student consent (plagiarism tools, not AI-specific).

units.why: The page says violations 'may result in appropriate academic penalties, including reduction of grade' and may follow the Code process; a general syllabus penalty template stating penalty types in advance, P37.
units.anchor: may result in appropriate academic penalties, including reduction of grade
units.policy: Violation of syllabus policies may result in appropriate academic penalties, including reduction of grade in the relevant assignment, project, test, or exam; if the Code of Student Academic Integrity is implicated, the process in the Code is followed.
units.fit_note: General syllabus-policy penalty language, not AI-specific; it also points to the Code process.

documents.title: Faculty FAQs: Artificial Intelligence
documents.summary: FAQ from the academic-integrity office explaining that no university-wide AI ban exists and faculty set expectations. It advises against relying on detectors, suggests talking with students, and lists faculty development.
documents.stance_why: It states 'Faculty have the discretion to set expectations for AI use in their courses' and 'there is no University-wide ban on AI tools', so the office hands the decision to instructors and sets none itself.

units.why: The FAQ says UNC Charlotte 'began its focused efforts early, hosting the first AI Summit in Spring 2023'; it narrates institutional engagement with faculty and leaders, with no rule. P88 (engaging peers and community) is the nearest.
units.anchor: hosting the first AI Summit in Spring 2023
units.policy: UNC Charlotte hosted the first AI Summit in Spring 2023 and continues to bring faculty and academic leaders together to build shared understanding and consistent guidance.
units.fit_note: Campus convenings of faculty and leaders rather than external coalitions.

units.why: The sentence says a 'faculty-led Task Force on AI in Teaching and Learning developed a comprehensive institutional roadmap'; this describes the body that produced university guidance, P84.
units.anchor: faculty‑led Task Force on AI in Teaching and Learning
units.policy: A faculty-led Task Force on AI in Teaching and Learning developed a comprehensive institutional roadmap for AI use and growth.

units.why: An AI Accelerator group 'in partnership with AAC&U' advances national-level work; a partnership with an outside association, P88.
units.anchor: in partnership with AAC&U, is advancing national‑level work
units.policy: A faculty-led AI Accelerator group, in partnership with AAC&U, is advancing national-level work on responsible and effective AI integration.

units.why: The university provides 'regular workshops on practical and pedagogical uses of AI' plus consultation with the integrity office to support faculty, P63.
units.anchor: regular workshops on practical and pedagogical uses of AI
units.policy: The university provides regular workshops on practical and pedagogical uses of AI, an annual AI Summit, and consultation services from Student Accountability & Conflict Resolution to support faculty.

units.why: 'we remain committed to adapting our guidance, resources, and support' states that guidance will change over time, P54.
units.anchor: we remain committed to adapting our guidance, resources, and support
units.policy: The university remains committed to adapting its guidance, resources and support as new issues emerge.

units.why: The FAQ recalls that the Code defines misconduct as behavior that 'interferes with the education or fair evaluation of a student's performance'; a generic definition that frames AI misuse, nearest P36, with AI only implied.
units.anchor: behaviors or actions by a student that interferes with the education or fair evaluation
units.policy: The Code of Student Academic Integrity defines academic misconduct as behaviors or actions by a student that interfere with the education or fair evaluation of a student's performance or work.
units.fit_note: General definition of misconduct; AI is only implied.

units.why: 'Faculty have the discretion to set expectations for AI use in their courses', so the decision is delegated to each instructor, P04.
units.anchor: Faculty have the discretion to set expectations for AI use
units.policy: Faculty have the discretion to set expectations for AI use in their courses.

units.why: 'Using AI tools without permission may constitute a policy violation, while using them within the faculty member's stated guidelines does not' links permission to misconduct, P36.
units.anchor: Using AI tools without permission may constitute a policy violation
units.policy: Using AI tools without permission may constitute a policy violation, while using them within the faculty member's stated guidelines does not.

units.why: 'there is no University-wide ban on AI tools' states the university's default: not prohibited, left to the course. P04 (decided by instructors) is nearer than P02 because AI is not welcomed, only not banned.
units.anchor: there is no University-wide ban on AI tools
units.policy: There is no University-wide ban on AI tools.
units.fit_note: States that no university-wide ban exists; the decision is left to faculty.

units.why: Faculty are 'encouraged to determine whether AI use is appropriate' based on 'learning objectives, subject-area considerations, and professional context'; AI decisions follow learning objectives, P83.
units.anchor: determine whether AI use is appropriate for their course, assignments, or assessments
units.policy: Faculty are encouraged to determine whether AI use is appropriate for their course, assignments, or assessments based on their learning objectives, subject-area considerations, and professional context.

units.why: The resources include guidance on 'setting tool permissions, assignment/exam statements, and sample AI Use/Disclosure statements'; the university offers templates and permission options for instructors, P05 as nearest.
units.anchor: setting tool permissions, assignment/exam statements, and sample AI Use/Disclosure statements
units.policy: Guidance is available to faculty on setting expectations with students, including tool permissions, assignment and exam statements, and sample AI Use/Disclosure statements.
units.fit_note: Offers resources and sample statements rather than named tiers.

units.why: 'we do not recommend faculty rely on detection tools' is a recommendation against relying on detectors, P39.
units.anchor: we do not recommend faculty rely on detection tools
units.policy: The university does not recommend that faculty rely on detection tools.

units.why: The reasons list 'Unreliable results, including false positives ... and false negatives'; a statement that detectors are unreliable, P39.
units.anchor: Unreliable results, including false positives
units.policy: Detection tools give unreliable results, including false positives (human work flagged as AI) and false negatives (AI-generated work going undetected).

units.why: 'Privacy concerns and risks when student work is uploaded into third-party systems' names a privacy risk of uploading student work, P50.
units.anchor: Privacy concerns and risks when student work is uploaded
units.policy: Uploading student work into third-party detection systems raises privacy concerns and risks.

units.why: 'We continue to monitor the marketplace' and tools need 'to be continuously vetted' describe ongoing review of detectors, a periodic re-evaluation of tools, P65.
units.anchor: We continue to monitor the marketplace and talk with other institutions
units.policy: The university continues to monitor the marketplace and talk with other institutions about detection tools to determine whether they are viable for the campus community.
units.fit_note: Ongoing review of detectors and consultation with peer institutions.

units.why: If work seems inconsistent with a student's ability, faculty should 'Invite the student to meet with you' and 'Ask about their process and drafts'; talking to the student before escalating, P57.
units.anchor: Invite the student to meet with you to discuss your concerns
units.policy: Faculty who have concerns about possible AI misuse invite the student to meet and discuss, and ask about their process and drafts and how they found resources or generated their reference list.

units.why: 'Redesigning assignments and assessments to require deeper, personalized evidence of student learning' and 'Assessing the process of learning' are assignment redesign, P35.
units.anchor: Redesigning assignments and assessments to require deeper, personalized evidence
units.policy: Some faculty redesign assignments and assessments to require deeper, personalized evidence of student learning and assess the process of learning, not just the product.

units.why: Faculty are described 'explaining why AI is appropriate or prohibited based on their learning objectives'; giving students the reasons for the rules, P66.
units.anchor: explaining why AI is appropriate or prohibited based on their learning objectives
units.policy: Some faculty provide clear expectations about acceptable AI use, promote transparency of use, and explain why AI is appropriate or prohibited based on their learning objectives.

units.why: Faculty are 'Teaching students what AI can do, its limitations, and how their profession defines ethical and acceptable use'; teaching about AI as a professional matter, P44.
units.anchor: Teaching students what AI can do, its limitations, and how their profession
units.policy: Some faculty teach students what AI can do, its limitations, and how their profession defines ethical and acceptable use.

units.why: 'Sharing strategies and insights with colleagues' and 'Participating in professional development opportunities like the AI Summit' describe peer learning among faculty, P63.
units.anchor: Participating in professional development opportunities like the AI Summit
units.policy: Some faculty share strategies with colleagues and take part in professional development such as the AI Summit and review Task Force and Accelerator reports.

units.why: The university lists CTL workshops, OneIT workshops and online courses and says 'Faculty are encouraged to pursue training, stay in conversation with peers'; support for faculty learning, P63.
units.anchor: Faculty are encouraged to pursue training, stay in conversation with peers
units.policy: Faculty are encouraged to pursue training, stay in conversation with peers, and share their experiences; development opportunities include Center for Teaching and Learning workshops, OneIT workshops, and online courses on generative AI usage and prompts.

documents.title: Office of Undergraduate Research AI policy
documents.summary: Policy of the Office of Undergraduate Research on AI in applications, proposals and OUR-supported research. AI is allowed as an assistive tool with prior mentor approval, disclosure and student ability to explain the work; full content generation and data fabrication are barred.
documents.stance_why: AI may assist writing and research but only with 'documented prior approval from their faculty mentor', must be disclosed, and 'AI must not be used to generate full sections'; it permits a short list of acceptable uses and bars others, which is restrict.

units.why: The policy says 'the responsibility for the work, learning, validity, authenticity, and accuracy always lies with the human researcher', putting ownership on the human; P29.
units.anchor: the responsibility for the work, learning, validity, authenticity, and accuracy
units.policy: The responsibility for the work, learning, validity, authenticity, and accuracy always lies with the human researcher.

units.why: 'Generative AI is not, and cannot be, a substitute for the human endeavor in creating and learning' says AI must not replace human thinking, P32.
units.anchor: Generative AI is not, and cannot be, a substitute for the human endeavor
units.policy: Generative AI is not, and cannot be, a substitute for the human endeavor in creating and learning.

units.why: The policy notes AI 'has unintended negative consequences on the environment, generating and disseminating misinformation' and asks each researcher to 'consider their use of AI tools carefully'; harms, P53.
units.anchor: unintended negative consequences on the environment, generating and disseminating misinformation
units.policy: The use of AI has unintended negative consequences on the environment, generating and disseminating misinformation, social and professional productivity, and the educational progress of users, so every researcher should consider their use of AI tools carefully and consistently with their core values.
units.fit_note: Also asks researchers to weigh AI use against their own values.

units.why: The text reports the university's 'commitment to the ethical and responsible use of artificial intelligence' and a vision of engaging with AI with high standards; an institutional framework statement, P56.
units.anchor: commitment to the ethical and responsible use of artificial intelligence
units.policy: The University has expressed a commitment to the ethical and responsible use of AI to enhance academic and administrative endeavors, and a vision of an environment where faculty, staff and students engage with AI to enhance teaching, learning, research and operations while upholding responsibility and integrity.

units.why: The OUR guidelines 'apply to the application process, program requirements, program management, recruitment and identification of students, and the research' of OUR-sponsored students; this sets the policy's scope, P61.
units.anchor: applies to the application process, program requirements, program management, recruitment
units.policy: OUR's guidelines apply to the application process, program requirements, program management, recruitment and identification of students, and the research OUR-sponsored students and mentors do.
units.fit_note: Defines scope of the unit policy rather than defining AI.

units.why: 'the student researcher must be able to understand, defend, and articulate their work, regardless of whatever tools they may use' requires explainability, P30.
units.anchor: must be able to understand, defend, and articulate their work
units.policy: The student researcher must be able to understand, defend, and articulate their work, regardless of whatever tools they may use to facilitate that research.

units.why: Generative AI in proposals, abstracts, posters, manuscripts and so on 'must adhere to the Code of Student Academic Integrity'; it ties AI use to the integrity code, P77.
units.anchor: must adhere to the Code of Student Academic Integrity
units.policy: Use of generative AI in research proposals, application essays, conference abstracts, presentations, posters, manuscripts, project reports, creative works and program reflections must adhere to the Code of Student Academic Integrity.

units.why: 'AI should enhance your understanding rather than be used as a shortcut that could limit the learning' warns that AI shortcuts learning, P41.
units.anchor: AI should enhance your understanding rather than be used as a shortcut
units.policy: When using AI for any purpose, students should integrate their personal knowledge and expertise; AI should enhance understanding rather than be a shortcut that could limit the learning and benefit from assignments.

units.why: 'AI-generated content may be used as a tool to assist ... but not as a replacement for original thought, analysis, and critical thinking' allows assistive use and bars replacing thinking; nearest P32.
units.anchor: not as a replacement for original thought, analysis, and critical thinking
units.policy: AI-generated content may be used as a tool to assist in the writing or research processes but not as a replacement for original thought, analysis, and critical thinking.
units.fit_note: Also permits AI as an assistive tool for writing and research.

units.why: 'must have documented prior approval from their faculty mentor' makes AI use conditional on mentor permission, so the mentor decides per project; P04.
units.anchor: must have documented prior approval from their faculty mentor
units.policy: Students using AI for a research project, a research manuscript, or creative work must have documented prior approval from their faculty mentor for the project.
units.fit_note: Requires documented prior approval by the faculty mentor, not an instructor's general rule.

units.why: 'final responsibility for the quality, accuracy, and academic integrity ... lies with the student' - students own the work, P29.
units.anchor: final responsibility for the quality, accuracy, and academic integrity
units.policy: The final responsibility for the quality, accuracy, and academic integrity of a research project, presentation, manuscript or creative work produced with AI assistance lies with the student.

units.why: 'If you cannot explain or demonstrate full understanding ... without AI support, you have gone beyond acceptable use' gives a test for acceptable use based on explainability, P30.
units.anchor: cannot explain or demonstrate full understanding of the content
units.policy: If a student cannot explain or demonstrate full understanding of the content of their proposal or project without AI support, they have gone beyond acceptable use.

units.why: AI use in a proposal, essay or abstract 'must be disclosed' and students must 'clearly identify which part(s)' were AI-generated, with citation; disclosure, P24, with part-level marking as fit note.
units.anchor: their use must be disclosed in the proposal/essay
units.policy: If AI tools are used in developing a research proposal, application essay, or conference abstract, their use must be disclosed in the proposal or essay, students must identify which parts were generated or significantly influenced by AI, and provide proper citation and attribution where appropriate.
units.fit_note: Requires identifying which parts of the work were AI-generated or influenced.

units.why: Reviewers are asked 'to refrain from uploading any content containing intellectual property submitted to OUR into any generative AI technology', protecting confidentiality; closest is P50, with the reviewer audience as fit note (P49 is about students and course materials).
units.anchor: refrain from uploading any content containing intellectual property submitted to OUR
units.policy: Reviewers refrain from uploading any content containing intellectual property submitted to OUR into any generative AI technology.
units.fit_note: Binds peer reviewers of proposals, to protect the confidentiality of submitted intellectual property.

units.why: 'OUR does not promote the use of generative AI tools during the peer-review process for analyzing or formulating peer-review critiques' is a research-review rule, P62.
units.anchor: does not promote the use of generative AI tools during the peer-review process
units.policy: OUR does not promote the use of generative AI tools during the peer-review process for analyzing or formulating peer-review critiques of grant applications or abstracts, to protect the intellectual confidentiality of proposals.

units.why: OUR states it may use generative AI 'to summarize review content for student feedback' and 'to organize and pre-categorize student applications', only consistent with OneIT's AI security checklist; staff use of AI in office operations, P76.
units.anchor: OUR may use AI to organize and pre-categorize student applications
units.policy: OUR may use generative AI to summarize review content for student feedback to protect reviewer identity and to organize and pre-categorize student applications to expedite evaluation, only in a manner consistent with OneIT's AI security checklist.
units.fit_note: Also requires consistency with OneIT's AI security checklist.

units.why: The examples list 'Brainstorming and Idea Generation' as acceptable, so AI may be used to explore directions; P15.
units.anchor: Using AI to help explore potential directions or organize thoughts
units.policy: Acceptable use of AI: brainstorming and idea generation, using AI to help explore potential directions or organize thoughts.

units.why: 'Editing Support: Using AI for grammar, spelling, clarity, tone, and readability improvements' is listed as acceptable; P91.
units.anchor: Using AI for grammar, spelling, clarity, tone, and readability improvements
units.policy: Acceptable use of AI: editing support, using AI for grammar, spelling, clarity, tone, and readability improvements.

units.why: 'Presentation Practice: Using AI to generate sample questions for Q&A or simulate practice sessions' is acceptable; practice and study aid, P14.
units.anchor: Using AI to generate sample questions for Q&A or simulate practice sessions
units.policy: Acceptable use of AI: presentation practice, using AI to generate sample questions for Q&A or simulate practice sessions.

units.why: 'Citation Checks: Using AI tools to verify formatting or suggest citation improvements' is acceptable; AI checking the student's own citations. P91 (editing support) is closest.
units.anchor: Using AI tools to verify formatting or suggest citation improvements
units.policy: Acceptable use of AI: citation checks, using AI tools to verify formatting or suggest citation improvements.
units.fit_note: Covers citation formatting checks rather than prose editing.

units.why: 'AI must not be used to generate full sections of your presentation's content or your abstract' bans AI producing submitted content, P19.
units.anchor: AI must not be used to generate full sections of your presentation’s content
units.policy: AI must not be used to generate full sections of your presentation's content or your abstract.

units.why: 'AI tools must not be used to fully design your research poster or slides without substantial human input and editing' bars AI producing the work wholesale; P19 with the human-input qualification as fit note.
units.anchor: must not be used to fully design your research poster or slides
units.policy: AI tools must not be used to fully design a research poster or slides without substantial human input and editing.
units.fit_note: Allows AI design help only with substantial human input and editing.

units.why: 'AI may not be used to fabricate data or perform analyses that misrepresent the project' is a ban on fabrication, P74.
units.anchor: AI may not be used to fabricate data or perform analyses that misrepresent
units.policy: AI may not be used to fabricate data or perform analyses that misrepresent the project.

units.why: 'Any substantial assistance from AI beyond the acceptable uses above must be disclosed to your mentor and may require acknowledgement' makes nondisclosure unacceptable; disclosure duty, P24.
units.anchor: must be disclosed to your mentor and may require acknowledgement
units.policy: Any substantial assistance from AI beyond the acceptable uses (brainstorming, editing, presentation practice, citation checks) must be disclosed to the mentor and may require acknowledgement on the presentation.
units.fit_note: Disclosure goes to the faculty mentor, and acknowledgement on the presentation is conditional.

units.why: The page says the policy was 'Adopted January 2026' and that its examples come from Purdue's Office of Undergraduate Research; provenance and date of the policy, P84.
units.anchor: Adopted January 2026
units.policy: The policy was adopted in January 2026, with examples of acceptable and unacceptable uses taken from Purdue University's Office of Undergraduate Research.

documents.title: Generative AI Usage Guidelines
documents.summary: OneIT's training deck for employees on generative AI: definitions, data and privacy rules, procurement, prompting advice and the approved campus tools. It is an IT and staff document with little on teaching or student coursework.
documents.stance_why: The deck sets data and tool-use guidance for employees and encourages experimentation ('If you are not sure how AI can help, experiment!') within data limits, and has no course-level stance. It gives no rule about coursework, so delegates fits; permit would overstate it because the main rules are data protection conditions.

units.why: The guidelines define AI as 'a computer's ability to perform tasks usually associated with human beings'; a definition setting scope, P61.
units.anchor: refers to a computer's ability to perform tasks usually associated with human beings
units.policy: Artificial Intelligence refers to a computer's ability to perform tasks usually associated with human beings like writing, creating images or videos, or performing data analysis.

units.why: Generative AI is defined as 'software applications ... that can generate text, images, videos, music'; a definition, P61.
units.anchor: refers specifically to software applications
units.policy: Generative AI is a branch of AI that refers specifically to software applications, like ChatGPT, Copilot and Adobe Firefly, that can generate text, images, videos, music, etc.

units.why: The slide lists benefits (productivity, personalized training, 24/7 support, improved research workflows, 'Prepare students to use AI in their field'); it names benefits of AI, P87.
units.anchor: AI tools can transform how we work, teach, and learn
units.policy: AI tools can transform how we work, teach, and learn: increase productivity on daily tasks, experience personalized training, provide personalized 24/7 support, improve research workflows, create text and media content, and prepare students to use AI in their field.
units.fit_note: Includes preparing students to use AI in their field (career skill).

units.why: 'Any individual using AI is responsible for understanding what data can be handled by the AI and what the AI is doing with the data' puts responsibility on the user for data; P50.
units.anchor: responsible for understanding what data can be handled by the AI
units.policy: Any individual using AI is responsible for understanding what data can be handled by the AI and what the AI is doing with the data.

units.why: 'Do not enter confidential or legally restricted data (e.g., ... FERPA, HIPAA ...) ... into an AI tool' is a data ban, P50.
units.anchor: Do not enter confidential or legally restricted data
units.policy: Do not enter confidential or legally restricted data (e.g., personnel records or data protected by FERPA, HIPAA, PCI) or any data that the data classification policy identifies as level 2 or 3 into an AI tool.

units.why: The exception that 'Level 2 data may be entered into the University's data-protected versions of Microsoft Copilot and Google Gemini' allows data in vetted tools, P50 (prefer vetted tools).
units.anchor: Level 2 data may be entered into the University’s data-
units.policy: Level 2 data may be entered into the University's data-protected versions of Microsoft Copilot and Google Gemini.

units.why: 'assume that any data or information you provide will be stored and made publicly available' warns that AI tools store prompts, P50.
units.anchor: assume that any data or information you provide will be stored
units.policy: When using AI tools, assume that any data or information you provide will be stored and made publicly available.

units.why: 'Read and review the University's Data Handling Guidelines' directs users to existing data policy, P77.
units.anchor: Read and review the University’s Data Handling Guidelines
units.policy: Users read and review the University's Data Handling Guidelines and do not enter level 2 or 3 data into an AI tool.
units.fit_note: Points to the data handling guidelines as the rule to follow.

units.why: 'Familiarize yourself with UNC Charlotte data retention policies when storing recordings and other AI outputs' ties AI outputs to existing retention rules, P77.
units.anchor: Familiarize yourself with UNC Charlotte data retention policies
units.policy: Users familiarize themselves with UNC Charlotte data retention policies when storing recordings and other AI outputs.

units.why: 'Always submit a procurement request even for free software so that OneIT and Legal affairs can review the data and privacy agreement' is institutional review of tools, P65.
units.anchor: Always submit a procurement request even for free software
units.policy: Users always submit a procurement request for any new AI tool, even free software, so that OneIT and Legal Affairs can review the data and privacy agreement.

units.why: 'Use solutions that have been reviewed and approved by the University when possible' tells users to prefer approved tools, P92 (institution-wide approved tools).
units.anchor: Use solutions that have been reviewed and approved by the University
units.policy: Use solutions that have been reviewed and approved by the University when possible.

units.why: The transparency slide says to 'Notify meeting participants if AI tools are being used in your meetings'; telling people when AI is in use, P103 (P86 concerns consent to recording, this is only notification).
units.anchor: Notify meeting participants if AI tools are being used
units.policy: Notify meeting participants if AI tools are being used in your meetings.
units.fit_note: Notice to meeting participants that AI tools are in use, with no consent requirement.

units.why: 'Cite AI tools that are used in the creation of content' and 'Acknowledge and document if AI tools are used to aid in writing and research' set disclosure duties, P24.
units.anchor: Cite AI tools that are used in the creation of content
units.policy: Cite AI tools that are used in the creation of content, and acknowledge and document if AI tools are used to aid in writing and research.

units.why: 'Inform stakeholders if AI tools are used to help draft documentation, policy, etc.' tells staff to disclose AI-drafted documents, P48 (disclosure of AI-made materials).
units.anchor: Inform stakeholders if AI tools are used to help draft documentation
units.policy: Inform stakeholders if AI tools are used to help draft documentation, policy, etc.
units.fit_note: Covers documents and policies drafted by staff, not only course materials.

units.why: 'Be mindful when using AI that can impact decisions, have ethical or legal ramifications, or infringe on the privacy of others' is a general responsible-use principle, P56.
units.anchor: Be mindful when using AI that can impact decisions
units.policy: Be mindful when using AI that can impact decisions, have ethical or legal ramifications, or infringe on the privacy of others.

units.why: 'Consumer AI tools store all of the data and information that you share. Avoid providing any information that should not be shared publicly' warns of storage, P50.
units.anchor: Consumer AI tools store all of the data and information
units.policy: Consumer AI tools store all of the data and information that you share, so avoid providing any information that should not be shared publicly; campus-wide approved tools provide data protection when used correctly.

units.why: 'it is up to you to determine how to best leverage them to augment your skills' and 'If you are not sure how AI can help, experiment!' encourage experimentation, P02.
units.anchor: If you are not sure how AI can help, experiment!
units.policy: Employees are encouraged to leverage AI to augment their skills and to experiment if unsure how AI can help.

units.why: The slide lists drafting uses: 'outlines for agendas, memos', 'social media posts', 'HTML code for web pages'. This permits AI drafting of text and some code; P91 (writing support) is closest, with HTML code as fit note.
units.anchor: AI tools can be used to draft content
units.policy: AI tools can be used to draft content such as outlines for agendas and memos, social media posts, and HTML code for web pages.
units.fit_note: Includes drafting HTML code and social media posts, beyond editing.

units.why: 'Always verify any content produced for accuracy, tone, and appropriate content' and 'you are the expert, not the AI tool' ask for verification, P31.
units.anchor: Always verify any content produced for accuracy, tone, and appropriate content
units.policy: Do not rely on AI to provide subject matter expertise or to be without bias; always verify any content produced for accuracy, tone, and appropriate content.

units.why: 'AI tools can produce biased results' names bias as a risk, P53.
units.anchor: AI tools can produce biased results
units.policy: AI tools can produce biased results.

units.why: 'AI tools may provide copyrighted material as part of their results' raises copyright concerns, P52.
units.anchor: AI tools may provide copyrighted material as part of their results
units.policy: AI tools may provide copyrighted material as part of their results, and it can be difficult to determine whether returned information falls under copyright protection.

units.why: The slide gives a three-part prompt model (background, core question, desired format) and says 'good outputs require good inputs'; prompting advice, P93.
units.anchor: good outputs require good inputs
units.policy: Provide clear and specific prompts to get the best results, consisting of background and role, a core question, and a desired format; revise the prompt if results are poor, and give an AI tool one primary task at a time.

units.why: 'The Office of OneIT maintains a curated list of AI tools that are available and approved for use across our campus' names the institutional approved tools, P92.
units.anchor: maintains a curated list of AI tools that are available and approved
units.policy: The Office of OneIT maintains a curated list of AI tools available and approved for use across campus, including CAISY AI Simulator, Microsoft Copilot in browser, Google Gemini, Adobe Firefly and Zoom AI Companion.

units.why: 'We encourage you to utilize campus-wide tools when possible' with a request form for new tools to 'ensure it meets our security standards'; prefer approved tools and review new ones, P92.
units.anchor: We encourage you to utilize campus-wide tools when possible
units.policy: Employees are encouraged to use campus-wide tools when possible; for a new tool believed to benefit their work they collaborate with their procurement officer and complete the Software and IT Request form to ensure it meets security standards.

notes: Coder B. No computing-unit or school-level policy collected. Syllabus page contains many non-AI notices that were not coded. OneIT guidelines are written for employees, so most units have actor all.
